summary:
Sara Hooker frames the talk around who gets to participate at the frontier of AI discovery. She notes modern computer science is only 77 years old—two generations—and that professionalization replaced gentleman scientists with an aggressively filtered system she and Rosanne Liu call the unreasonably narrow path: the right PhD, the right industry lab, the right problem at the right time. Compute compounded this, creating a GPU-poor versus GPU-rich divide, concentrating breakthroughs in a handful of frontier labs, and leaving entire regions of the world statistically absent from discovery maps.

She offers two reasons the funnel is widening. First, AutoScientist automates model training by co-optimizing the entire loop from data through alignment, self-evolving per domain. It outperforms research staff because humans carry priors about specific architectures while the search ranges across model sizes and dense versus mixture-of-experts designs. Critically, it only paid off once they controlled data quality alongside the model rather than leaving data decisions to the agent. Win rates sat just above 60% because that was the budget stopping point; removing that ceiling let performance keep climbing. Demand is most acute in medical, legal, science, and code domains. They cover 242 languages from day one and focus on non-verifiable tasks.

Second, her slow death of scaling argument holds that pretraining size is no longer the most lucrative axis of scale. LLM leaderboards show the ratio of best small models under 13B versus larger models flipping over time. Returns now come from a broader action space where recipe and algorithm matter again, and barriers to entry are more nimble. Current architecture is saturated; no frontier lab will quadruple model size for pretraining. Architecture determines the ceiling, and we are at the size ceiling. This matters for access because pretraining compute must be colocated and enormous, while the compute that now pays off—agentic and post-training—is distributable and doesn't require GPU hoarding.

In Q&A, Hooker elaborates that fewer than 5,000 people worldwide know how to train frontier models at scale, and that knowledge travels like an apprenticeship; automating it accelerates innovation cycles. The cost of asking shapes what gets asked, so cheaper asking changes the volume of questions. On safety and open source, she gives a nuanced answer acknowledging risk but noting that restricting access also limits who can participate. On parametric versus non-parametric storage, she notes co-optimization of data and model is essential and that co-training choices is a long-horizon problem. On distillation, she agrees larger models still matter but argues we've hit the size ceiling for current architecture, so innovation happens within that ceiling. AutoScientist is in beta with free GPUs offered.

sections.title: Seventy seven years of computer science and the unreasonably narrow path
sections.summary: Hooker frames the history of computer science as only 77 years old and traces how discovery shifted from gentleman scientists to professionalized labs, creating what she and Rosanne Liu call the unreasonably narrow path: the right PhD, the right industry lab, the right problem at the right time.

sections.title: GPU poor vs GPU rich and geographic inequality in breakthroughs
sections.summary: Compute compounded the narrow path, creating a GPU-poor versus GPU-rich divide. A handful of frontier labs build the technology everyone uses, and Stanford's map of significant breakthroughs shows entire regions of the world completely left out.

sections.title: Ripe for a revolution and AutoScientist
sections.summary: Hooker introduces AutoScientist, which automates model training by co-optimizing the entire loop from data through alignment and self-evolving per domain. It outperforms research staff because it searches across model sizes and dense vs mixture-of-experts designs without human architectural priors. It only worked once data quality was co-optimized with the model.

sections.title: The 60% budget stop and domain demand
sections.summary: Win rates sat just above 60% because that was the budget stopping point; removing it let rates keep climbing. AutoScientist changes many hyperparameters simultaneously. Demand is most acute in medical, legal, science, and code domains. They cover 242 languages from day one and focus on non-verifiable tasks.

sections.title: The slow death of scaling and broader action space
sections.summary: Hooker argues pretraining size is no longer the most lucrative axis of scale because the current architecture is saturated. Smaller models outperform larger ones. This matters for access because pretraining compute must be colocated and enormous while the compute that now pays off is distributable and higher return per flop.

sections.title: Small models overtaking larger ones and the broader action space
sections.summary: LLM leaderboards show the ratio of best small models under 13B versus larger models flipping over time. Returns now come from a broader action space where recipe and algorithm matter again, with more nimble barriers to entry. Hooker argues this is a good time to work on intelligence because the question matters more than the credential.

sections.title: Q&A: Democratization and the cost of asking
sections.summary: Hooker explains democratization is twofold: fewer than 5,000 people know how to train frontier models at scale and that knowledge is apprenticeship-like, so automating it accelerates innovation cycles. The cost of asking shapes what gets asked; cheaper asking changes the volume of questions. Agentic and post-training compute doesn't require GPU hoarding, giving people with the best ideas a higher chance of winning.

sections.title: Q&A: Safety, open source, and parametric storage
sections.summary: On safety and open source, Hooker acknowledges risk but notes that restricting access also limits who can participate. AutoScientist is about enabling customization and ownership of intelligence. On parametric versus non-parametric storage, she notes co-optimization of data and model is essential and co-training choices is a long-horizon problem.

sections.title: Q&A: Distillation, size ceiling, and AutoScientist beta
sections.summary: Hooker agrees larger models still matter for distillation but argues no frontier lab will quadruple model size for pretraining because current architecture is at its size ceiling. Data quality means capacity is used more efficiently, with post-training moving further back as a bigger lever. AutoScientist is in beta with free GPUs offered to remove the compute hurdle.
